In mathematics, the '''conformal dimension''' of a [[metric space]] ''X'' is the infimum of the [[Hausdorff dimension]] over the [[conformal gauge]] of ''X'', that is, the class of all metric spaces [[quasisymmetric map|quasisymmetric]] to&nbsp;''X''.<ref>John M. Mackay, Jeremy T. Tyson, ''Conformal Dimension : Theory and Application'', University Lecture Series, Vol. 54, 2010, Rhodes Island</ref>

==Formal definition==

Let ''X'' be a metric space and <math>\mathcal{G}</math> be the collection of all metric spaces that are quasisymmetric to&nbsp;''X''. The conformal dimension of ''X'' is defined as such

: <math> \mathrm{Cdim} X = \inf_{Y \in \mathcal{G}} \dim_H Y</math>

==Properties==

We have the following [[Inequality (mathematics)|inequalities]], for a metric space&nbsp;''X'':

: <math>\dim_T X \leq \mathrm{Cdim} X \leq \dim_H X</math>

The second inequality is true by definition.  The first one is deduced from the fact that the [[topological dimension]] is invariant by [[homeomorphism]] and it is always smaller than or equal to the [[Hausdorff dimension]].

==Examples==

* The conformal dimension of <math>\mathbf{R}^N</math> is ''N'', since the topological and Hausdorff dimensions of [[Euclidean space]]s agree.
* The [[Cantor set]] ''K'' is of null conformal dimension.  However, there is no metric space quasisymmetric to ''K'' with a 0 Hausdorff dimension.
